Glorious Return
glōr'ee-əs ri-tĕrn'
n. (the armed return of the exiled Waldenses from Switzerland to their Alpine valleys in August 1689, under Henri Arnaud)
French Glorieuse Rentrée, the glorious re-entry, the Waldenses' own name for it.

Definition · Webster 1828 · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The Glorious Return was the march by which the Waldenses recovered their homeland. In January 1686, under pressure from Louis XIV, Duke Victor Amadeus II of Savoy ordered the Protestants of the Piedmont valleys to abandon their faith or leave. Those who resisted were overwhelmed; some two thousand were killed, more than eight thousand imprisoned in the duke's fortresses, where many died, and in 1687 the survivors, perhaps three thousand, were released into exile in Switzerland. On the night of 16–17 August 1689, some nine hundred of the exiles, led by their pastor Henri Arnaud, crossed Lake Geneva in boats from Prangins and marched for twelve days over the high Alpine passes, fighting their way through Savoyard and French troops, until they reached the valleys of Piedmont. Through the winter they held the rock fortress of the Balsiglia above the Germanasca valley against an army many times their number; in May 1690, when the French brought cannon and the last assault was expected, the defenders escaped through the fog by night. Weeks later Victor Amadeus broke with France and joined the Grand Alliance, made peace with the Waldenses, and allowed the exiles to come home. They had prayed with Israel in exile, “If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning” (Psa 137:5).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines exile as banishment, the state of being expelled from one's country, and return as the act of coming back.

expand to see more

EX'ILE, n. Banishment; the state of being expelled from one's native country or place of residence.

RETURN', n. The act of returning or coming back to the same place or condition.

FOR'TRESS, n. Any fortified place; a fort; a castle; a stronghold.

Psa 137:5 — "If I forget thee, O Jerusalem, let my right hand forget her cunning."

Isa 35:10 — "And the ransomed of the LORD shall return, and come to Zion with songs and everlasting joy upon their heads: they shall obtain joy and gladness, and sorrow and sighing shall flee away."

Modern Corruption

Nine hundred Waldensian exiles who marched home over the Alps and held their valleys.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The Glorious Return is a story of providence before it is a story of arms. A small company of exiles with no hope of victory held out until a political reversal no one foresaw opened the way home, and the Waldenses themselves read it so: “If it had not been the LORD who was on our side, when men rose up against us” (Psa 124:2).

The principle to recover is the hope of the prophets for a scattered people: “there is hope in thine end, saith the LORD, that thy children shall come again to their own border” (Jer 31:17). The church's earthly homes are given and taken by God, and the Return foreshadows the greater return of Isa 35:10, when “the ransomed of the LORD shall return, and come to Zion with songs” (Isa 35:10).
